Volume 13 · Chapter 11

Matching, networks and market design

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v13-c10

By the endAnalyze stable allocations and strategic interactions on markets and networks.

Volume 13 · Chapter 11

Choose the allocation rule, the payment rights and the network

An allocation office can assign placements by reported preferences, sell owned resources at prices, or support collaboration among people who affect one another’s returns. These are different economic problems. A stable placement need not maximize a sum of monetary values; an efficient assignment needs an actual payment rule; and a welfare-improving network may never form through individually attractive steps. The design question begins by specifying what each participant can choose and which changes require someone else’s consent.

Capability. Prove applicant deferred acceptance is individually strategy-proof in a finite strict one-to-one market, including incomplete lists and outside options; certify efficient monetary assignments; and solve network games and link-formation problems with explicit global, boundary and financing arguments. Six original cases and twelve solved exercises distinguish these claims.

Prerequisites. The introductory matching chapter established deferred-acceptance stability and proposer optimality while deferring the full incentive proof. Sections 1–3 below close that proof. Static games supplies Nash equilibrium and best replies; Mechanism design and auctions supplies the distinction between a type, an admissible report and a payment rule. Basic finite linear algebra and quadratic completion are used explicitly. All examples here are synthetic models, not measured market outcomes.

1. Strict matching with an outside option

Let A be a finite set of applicants and H a finite set of institutions with one place each. Their sizes need not agree; either set may be empty. Each agent has a strict preference order over members of the opposite side and the outside outcome ∅, meaning unmatched. A partner is acceptable exactly when ranked above ∅. We encode a report as an ordered subset of acceptable names. All omitted names are below outside; their relative order is irrelevant to the algorithm. A false report may reorder names, omit a truly acceptable name, or declare a truly unacceptable name acceptable.

A matching μ is a partial bijection: μ(a)=h if and only if μ(h)=a; otherwise μ(i)=∅. There are no payments, matching externalities or couples. An agent compares matchings solely by its own assigned partner. Individual rationality means nobody is matched to an unacceptable partner. An unmatched applicant and an empty institution are permitted outcomes. A pair (a,h) blocks μ if both strictly prefer each other to their assigned partner or outside. A matching is stable when it is individually rational and has no blocking pair. Stability tests permitted bilateral deviations; it is neither a statement about every coalition nor a numerical welfare sum.

In applicant-proposing deferred acceptance, abbreviated APDA, select any unmatched applicant with an untried acceptable name. It proposes to its highest remaining name. That institution retains its favorite acceptable proposal among its existing hold and the new offer, rejecting the rest. An unacceptable proposal is rejected immediately. Continue until no eligible proposal remains; make the holds final. These proposals are steps in a computation on reports, not binding offers that a proposer can strategically withdraw while the algorithm runs. Institution-proposing DA, IPDA, interchanges the two sides.

Termination and stability. Every ordered proposer–recipient pair is tried at most once, so at most |A||H| proposals occur. A recipient’s held partner only improves in its strict order; after accepting someone acceptable it never returns to unmatched. Final individual rationality follows from the proposal and retention rules. If (a,h) blocked the final outcome, a would have proposed to h before its final, less-preferred partner, or before exhausting its list. Institution h rejected a immediately or later and thereafter held someone strictly better. Its final partner is therefore better than a, contradicting blocking. The proof applies to either proposing side and includes empty lists.

The first rejected achievable pair. Call (a,h) achievable if it occurs in some stable matching for this fixed profile. Suppose some achievable pair is rejected, and take the first such rejection. Let ν be stable with ν(a)=h. Rejection cannot be for unacceptability, because ν is individually rational. Institution h instead holds b≠a, whom it strictly prefers to a. To have proposed to h, b has already been rejected by every institution it ranks above h. If ν(b) were above h, that earlier rejection would itself concern an achievable pair, contrary to our choice of the first one. It cannot equal h, since ν(a)=h. If ν(b)=∅, b still prefers h because it proposed only to acceptable names. Thus b strictly prefers h to ν(b), and h prefers b to ν(h)=a. Pair (b,h) blocks ν: a contradiction.

No proposer is ever rejected by an achievable partner. Consequently APDA gives each applicant a partner weakly preferred to its partner in any stable matching. This is proposer optimality. It also proves schedule independence: each legal proposal schedule yields a stable proposer-optimal outcome; strict preferences imply that any two such outcomes assign the same partner to every proposer and hence are the same matching. This establishes an outcome independent of how we queue eligible proposals.

The definitions and rejection argument can be compared with Manea’s matching slides, dated 27 June 2016. Proposer optimality concerns stable matchings for one fixed reported profile. A lie changes that profile. Therefore this result alone is not a proof that truth-telling is optimal.

2. A complete proof of proposer strategy-proofness

We fix every applicant’s report except applicant i’s and fix all institutions’ strict priority and acceptability lists. The other reports need not be truthful. We will construct one set Si, independent of i’s report, and prove that APDA always assigns i its reported-best element of that set. Truth then selects its true best element. The construction requires a finite unmatched-set lemma, not an assumption about incentives.

The same agents are unmatched in every stable matching

Suppose μ and ν are stable for the same profile, μ(m0)=∅, and ν(m0)=h0. By individual rationality m0 prefers h0 to outside. Stability of μ forces h0 to have a partner m1 whom it prefers to m0; otherwise that pair blocks μ. Since ν(h0)=m0, stability of ν forces m1 to have a partner h1 whom it prefers to h0. The partner must exist, because h0 is acceptable to m1. Stability of μ now forces h1 to have a partner m2 whom it prefers to m1. Continue alternately:

hk=ν(mk),   mk+1=μ(hk),
hk≻mₖμ(mk),   mk+1≻hₖν(hk).

Every next partner exists by the preceding strict preference and stability. Nor can the path close into a cycle. At a first repeated applicant mk+1=mj, j=0 would give m0 a μ-partner, contradicting μ(m0)=∅. If j>0, injectivity of μ gives hk=hj−1; injectivity of ν then gives mk=mj−1, an earlier repeated applicant. This contradicts the definition of the first repeat. Finiteness makes an indefinitely extending path of distinct applicants impossible. Thus no applicant is unmatched only in μ. Swap μ and ν for the reverse inclusion, and interchange applicants and institutions for the same conclusion on the other side. Every stable matching has exactly the same unmatched agents. This is the finite one-to-one result just proved; no hospital-capacity extension is being invoked.

Construct a menu without asking i for a report

Run IPDA with i rejecting every proposal. Define Si to contain outside and every institution that proposes to i during this reject-all run. Its computation never uses i’s preferences. If we delete the futile proposals to i, the remaining steps form a legal IPDA run with i removed. By schedule independence its final matching is the unique IPDA outcome ν−i of that smaller market. Institutions propose in descending acceptable order, so

Si={∅} ∪ {h∈H : i≻hν−i(h)}.

If h is unmatched in the smaller market, the comparison is with outside. An institution that finds i unacceptable cannot be in the second set. An institution that proposes to i in the reject-all run subsequently moves only downward on its list, so i ranks above its final partner. Conversely, if i ranks above that final partner, or above outside when h exhausts its list, h must have tried i. This proves the displayed equivalence, including empty institutions. The menu may contain institutions that i truly finds unacceptable; outside will protect i against them under a truthful report.

Every actual APDA partner is in this menu

For any ordered-subset report Pi, let h*=APDAi(Pi,P−i). If h*=∅, it is already in Si. Otherwise take the full APDA matching and replace i’s report by the singleton list [h*]. That matching is still individually rational and stable: i keeps its only acceptable partner, deleting other acceptable names cannot create an i-blocking pair, and everyone else’s assignments and comparisons are unchanged. By the unmatched-set lemma, IPDA on the singleton problem must also match i, necessarily to h*.

Couple that singleton IPDA run with the reject-all run: choose the same free institution for the next proposal as long as the histories agree. Before the first offer from h*, i rejects every offer in both runs, so all responses agree. The singleton run must eventually receive h*’s offer to finish matched. Therefore the reject-all run receives the same offer. Hence h*∈Si. This argument used stability and the proved unmatched-set lemma, not strategy-proofness.

No menu member is reported better than the actual partner

First suppose h* is an institution. Truncate Pi to the names strictly above h*, deleting h* and every lower name. Call the resulting list Ti. Take a legal full APDA execution and reproduce its prefix up to just before i’s first proposal to its final partner h*. Every earlier proposal by i is to a member of Ti and has been rejected; all those proposals and responses remain legal and identical in the truncated problem. At that point i is unmatched and has exhausted its entire truncated list. It makes no further proposals and remains unmatched while the other applicants finish. This constructs a stable truncated-problem outcome with i unmatched. If h*=∅, take Ti to be the original entire acceptable list; the original final outcome already leaves i unmatched.

The unmatched-set lemma implies that IPDA on the Ti problem leaves i unmatched as well. Now i is a receiver. Once it accepts an acceptable offer, it always holds one: it can only upgrade, and a held proposer does not withdraw. Thus the truncated IPDA run never receives an offer belonging to Ti. Couple it with reject-all up to a first such offer. All responses before that event would agree, so the event would occur in both or neither. It occurs in neither. Therefore Si contains no institution strictly Pi-preferred to h*.

The incentive theorem. The two arguments show, for every report Pi, that APDA selects the Pi-best element of the fixed set Si, where outside is included. A truthful report therefore selects the true-preference maximum over all outcomes any unilateral report can induce. No lie can strictly improve the applicant’s true outcome. This is individual strategy-proofness, or weak dominance of truthful reporting, in the full ordered-subset report domain. It covers arbitrary reordering, truncation, an empty list and falsely acceptable names. It does not assert that every lie hurts, that recipients are strategy-proof, or that coalitions cannot manipulate.

This route is developed from the noncircular Appendix B of Gonczarowski, Heffetz and Thomas, version 4 dated 9 September 2026. Their main-text menu proof assumes the known incentive theorem; it would be circular for our purpose. Here the finite unmatched-set lemma and the singleton and truncation couplings have been supplied explicitly. The theorem remains confined to strict one-to-one matching without externalities; ties, capacities, couples and contracts require their own domains and proofs.

3. An outside option can be the best attainable outcome

Worked case 1: four applicants, three places

Read each list from best to worst. Omitted names are unacceptable; outside lies below every listed name. There is one seat at each institution.

Original incomplete placement market
ApplicantAcceptable institutionsInstitutionAcceptable applicants
AX, YXB, A
BY, XYA, B
CZZC, D
DZ——

APDA immediately gives A–X and B–Y. C and D both seek Z, which retains C. The result is μ=(A–X,B–Y,C–Z,D–∅). Under IPDA, X first proposes to B, Y to A and Z to C, giving ν=(A–Y,B–X,C–Z,D–∅). Both are stable. To show the list is complete, observe that any stable matching must fill Z with C: if Z is empty or holds D, C and Z block. Both A and B must be matched within {X,Y}, because a vacant institution and an unmatched mutually acceptable applicant would block. The only two bijections of that submarket are the displayed assignments. Thus there are exactly 2 stable matchings, not merely two examples of stable matchings.

The fixed menu of A is {∅,X,Y}, and that of B is {∅,X,Y}. For example, remove A and run IPDA: X and Y both propose to B, who keeps Y and rejects X. The final smaller-market outcome has X empty, Y–B and Z–C. Institution X prefers A to outside, and Y prefers A to B, so both belong to A’s menu. C’s menu is {∅,Z}. D’s is {∅}: when D is removed, Z already obtains C, whom it prefers to D. Truth therefore gives D its best attainable outcome, although that outcome is unmatched. This is not a guarantee that every applicant obtains a place.

A complete finite check enumerates 21 individually rational partial matchings: seven partial matchings in the A,B–X,Y submarket times three choices for Z (empty, C or D). Testing every mutually acceptable pair leaves exactly μ and ν. Over three institutions there are 1+3+6+6=16 ordered-subset reports, so 64 unilateral reports across the four applicants. Each reproduces its report-best fixed-menu choice. The general incentive proof does not depend on this finite verification.

Changed institution. If C is removed, D gets Z. If C remains but Z’s priority is reversed to D above C, D again gets Z and C becomes unmatched. Neither change is a preference lie by D with the rest of the environment held fixed. As a separate boundary example, one applicant who truly finds the only institution unacceptable receives outside when truthful; falsely listing that institution can produce a worse match if it accepts the applicant. Including outside in the proof matters.

4. Which messages and whose incentives?

Worked case 2: a recipient’s lie and an applicant’s short list

This is a different market. All four partners on each list are acceptable; outside comes last.

A four-by-four rejection chain
ApplicantInstitutionsInstitutionApplicants
AX, Y, Z, WXC, A, D, B
BY, Z, X, WYA, B, C, D
CZ, X, Y, WZB, C, A, D
DX, W, Y, ZWD, A, B, C

Truthful APDA gives (A–X,B–Y,C–Z,D–W): X holds A rather than D, and D goes to W. IPDA gives (A–Y,B–Z,C–X,D–W), because every institution obtains its first choice. These are the only stable matchings. First, an incomplete matching cannot be stable in this complete balanced market: an unmatched applicant and empty institution would block. D cannot be at X, since A ranks X first and X prefers A to D, so (A,X) would block. D cannot be at Y or Z, since it prefers W and W ranks D first, so (D,W) would block. Thus D must be at W. Of the six remaining assignments of X,Y,Z to A,B,C, XYZ and YZX are stable; XZY is blocked by (C,X), YXZ by (B,Z), ZXY by (A,X), and ZYX by (A,Y). This exhausts the feasible alternatives. The finite checker also tests all 209 partial matchings, including those immediately excluded by this observation.

Allow only X to report C,D,A,B instead of its true C,A,D,B. When D proposes, X now holds D and rejects A. A moves to Y, displacing B; B moves to Z, displacing C; C moves to X, displacing D; D goes to W. The resulting matching is the second one above. X has improved in its true order from A to C. The applicant theorem says nothing about this recipient deviation. We have exhibited one manipulable recipient, not proved a universal impossibility statement about every matching mechanism.

With truthful institution lists fixed, the institution portions of the applicants’ menus are A:{X,Y,W}, B:{Y,Z}, C:{X,Z}, D:{W}; add outside to each. Every one of the 1+4+12+24+24=65 possible ordered lists can be checked, totaling 260 unilateral reports. Menus are possible outcomes across changed reports, not merely partners occurring in stable matchings for the true profile. A’s menu includes W, even though A gets neither W in the two true-profile stable outcomes.

Now impose a one-name report cap. A,B,C,D sincerely list X,Y,Z,X, respectively. The result leaves D unmatched. D can instead submit the permitted list [W] and obtain W. “Report your true first choice” is therefore not a dominant instruction in this capped domain. The full true ordering was not an admissible message. If the cap is two and everyone lists its true first two, D can list X,W and the original APDA outcome returns. A cap change, recipient manipulation and applicant misreporting in the unrestricted domain are three distinct experiments.

5. Assignments with prices and owned resources

Consider a separate finite resource market. Each buyer can obtain at most one object; each object can have at most one buyer. Buyer i values object j at vij in quasilinear utility units and can decline for incremental utility zero. Each object belongs to its own seller, whose retention value is zero. If the buyer pays pj, its utility increment is vij−pj, and the seller receives that payment. There may be a declared set of forbidden buyer–object pairs. Monetary values and transfers are meaningful here; adding or comparing ordinal placement ranks from the previous sections would not produce this model.

A global price certificate. Choose nonnegative numbers ui,pj satisfying ui+pj≥vij on every allowed edge. For any feasible partial assignment M,

Σ(i,j)∈M vij ≤ Σi matchedui+Σj soldpj ≤ Σiui+Σjpj.

The first inequality uses the edge constraints and the second uses nonnegativity and the one-unit resource limits. If a candidate assignment has equality on each assigned edge, ui=0 for every unmatched buyer and pj=0 for every unsold object, it attains the bound. It therefore maximizes total value over all partial assignments. Every assigned buyer obtains its best allowed value minus price and weakly prefers buying to outside. Every unmatched buyer has no positive-surplus allowed object. Nonnegative prices and zero retention values make sellers willing to sell, and an unsold object is priced at zero. These statements form a competitive supporting-price certificate.

This proof is just a sum of inequalities. A finite set of assignments always has a value maximizer; we have not shown that every possible assignment problem has supporting prices, nor invoked general linear-programming integrality. The welfare sum includes sellers: each payment subtracts from one party and adds to another. This model and that cancellation are discussed in Pass’s matching-markets chapter, Sections 8.1–8.3.

Worked case 3: a certificate that survives a forbidden edge

Three buyers each own 20 units of currency. Sellers X,Y,Z each own the corresponding one-unit object; no buyer’s displayed payment is liquidity constrained. Valuations are:

Original unit-demand values
BuyerXYZ
A1282
B1065
C497

Choose prices p=(5,2,0) and buyer utilities u=(7,5,7). The nine values ui+pj are rows (12,9,7), (10,7,5), (12,9,7), each weakly above its valuation row. Assignment A–X, B–Z, C–Y has equality on every chosen edge. Its value is 12+5+9=26, exactly Σu+Σp=19+7. Thus it is globally optimal, including against partial allocations. The six full-assignment values, in order XYZ, XZY, YXZ, YZX, ZXY, ZYX for A,B,C, are 25,26,25,17,21,12. Every value is positive, so a partial assignment can be extended to a full one with higher total value. The optimum is unique.

The payment ledger matters. A pays seller X 5, B pays seller Z 0 and C pays seller Y 2. Buyer cash closes at (15,20,18); seller cash receipts, in X,Y,Z order, are (5,2,0). Total cash remains 60. Buyer utility increments total 19 and seller receipts total 7, giving social value 26. Seller Z is indifferent about selling for zero; that tie is allowed. Although B also demands X and C also demands Z at these prices, the displayed chosen allocation clears the market.

Change one resource constraint. Forbid B–Z. The optimal value falls to 25, attained by exactly A–X/B–Y/C–Z and A–Y/B–X/C–Z. Prices (6,2,0) and utilities (6,4,7) give rows (12,8,6), (10,6,4), (13,9,7). All allowed-edge inequalities hold and the chosen edges attain equality in both allocations. The B–Z inequality fails, 4<5, but it is no longer an allowed allocation. The total bound is 17+8=25. All nine original values are positive and the direct certificate covers the 27 allowed partial assignments; no extension argument through a forbidden edge is needed. At zero prices both A and B would most want X. An efficient allocation without supporting prices is not automatically a decentralized clearing outcome.

6. Best replies on a fixed network

A matching specifies a partner; a network can connect one person to several neighbors. For a fixed directed coefficient matrix B with bii=0, consider nonnegative actions and payoffs

ui(x)=aixi−xi2/2+xiΣj≠ibijxj,   xi≥0.

The finite coefficients are common knowledge. Each person selects one action simultaneously, holding others’ actions fixed when considering a deviation. These are monetary-equivalent effort benefits and disutility, not a dated schedule of cash receipts and invoices. A later transfer policy will have a separate cash ledger. The cross derivative bij measures strategic complementarity when positive and substitution when negative. In these particular payoffs it also controls the direction of the payoff externality, ∂ui/∂xj=bijxi. Those two concepts need not coincide in other payoff specifications.

Completing the square in xi proves the unique global best reply

Ri(x)=max{0,ai+Σjbijxj}.

The own-action second derivative is −1, so a nonnegative stationary action is globally optimal and a negative stationary action is replaced by zero. A pure Nash equilibrium is a fixed point of this complete best-response map. Solving the unrestricted linear equations without checking signs would omit this boundary condition. Network games with this structure and their active-set restrictions are studied in Bramoullé, Kranton and D’Amours’s 2014 article. Our small games below are solved directly, including their exceptional parameters.

A sufficient contraction theorem on an unbounded action set. Put q=maxiΣj|bij|. Because z↦max(0,z) is 1-Lipschitz, ||R(x)−R(y)||∞≤q||x−y||∞. Assume q<1. Starting from any x0≥0, define xk+1=R(xk). If d=||x1−x0||∞, induction gives ||xk+1−xk||∞≤qkd. For m>k, the triangle inequality yields

||xm−xk||∞ ≤ d Σr=km−1qr ≤ dqk/(1−q).

Each coordinate is therefore a Cauchy sequence of real numbers. Its limit is nonnegative, so x* lies in the closed orthant. Continuity gives R(x*)=x*. If y* were another fixed point, ||x*−y*||≤q||x*−y*|| forces equality of the two vectors. This proves existence, uniqueness and convergence of this specified synchronous iteration; compactness of the orthant was never assumed. At q=0 the map is constant and the result is immediate. Clipping best replies at finite upper bounds preserves the same Lipschitz bound. A failed sufficient bound q<1 proves neither multiplicity nor nonexistence.

Worked case 4: complementary effort and the cost of implementation

Take the three-node path 1—2—3, ai=1 and bij=βGij, where G has ones on the two undirected edges, zeros elsewhere, and β≥0. Begin with the unbounded action set xi≥0. At β=1/4, q=1/2, so the preceding theorem applies. Best replies are strictly positive. The equations x1=1+βx2=x3 and x2=1+β(x1+x3) give

xN=(10/7,12/7,10/7),   u(xN)=(50/49,72/49,50/49),   W(xN)=172/49.

At a positive best reply, the linear marginal term equals xi, so ui=xi2/2; this checks all three payoffs. The aggregate welfare and the game’s potential are different quadratic functions:

W(x)=Σui(x)=1′x−x′(I−2βG)x/2,
Φ(x)=1′x−x′(I−βG)x/2.

For symmetric G, ∂Φ/∂xi is the individual marginal payoff, whereas ∂W/∂xi includes effects on neighbors as well. Each undirected cross benefit occurs in both endpoints’ payoffs. At β=1/4 set Q=I−G/2. Its quadratic form satisfies

z′Qz=(z1−z2/2)2+(z3−z2/2)2+z22/2.

This is strictly positive for nonzero z. Solving Qx*=1 gives (3,4,3). The exact identity W(x*)−W(x)=(x−x*)′Q(x−x*)/2 proves global, unique optimality on the whole orthant, not just stationarity. Gross utility increments are (3/2,2,3/2), and total welfare is 5. The welfare gain is 73/49. It is not yet an implemented policy.

A fully financed policy variant. Now explicitly restrict actions to [0,4] and give each person 10 units of cash. The old Nash actions and the planner target remain feasible. Set per-unit subsidies s=(1,3/2,1). After observing all actions, first collect

chargei(x)=½Σj≠isjxj,
then pay subsidyi(x)=sixi.

The charges are at most (5,4,5), so initial cash pays them before any subsidy arrives. For every allowed action profile, Σcharge=Σsubsidy: each subsidy appears in exactly two charges with coefficient 1/2. The pool starts and ends with zero and needs no outside subsidy. Effort benefits and disutility are the utility function above; they are not additional cash invoices credited against these funding bounds. Each charge is independent of its own payer’s action. Individual best replies therefore become min{4,max{0,1+si+βΣGijxj}}, still a contraction with q=1/2. The target (3,4,3) satisfies these best replies and is their unique fixed point.

At that target the subsidies are (3,6,3), charges are (9/2,3,9/2), and net transfers are (−3/2,3,−3/2). Cash closes at (17/2,13,17/2), totaling the original 30. After transfers, utility increments relative to initial cash are (0,5,0). Both endpoints lose relative to their original 50/49, despite the rise in aggregate welfare. This design assumes compulsory enforceable charges; it is not a voluntary Pareto improvement. The cap and initial cash make the financing statement valid at every permitted profile, not just at equilibrium.

Change the feedback, then change the action set. Return to the original unbounded game. All equilibrium actions must be positive since every best reply is at least 1. The leaf actions coincide, and substitution gives (1−2β2)x1=1+β. For 0≤β<1/√2 this produces the unique positive equilibrium; for β≥1/√2 the left side is nonpositive at a positive x1 while the right side is positive, so no finite equilibrium exists. At β=3/5 the unique equilibrium is (40/7,55/7,40/7), even though q=6/5 fails the sufficient contraction condition. At β=3/4 the formal linear solution (-14,-20,-14) is infeasible; it is not a Nash outcome.

If instead actions are capped at 2 when β=3/4, every best reply lies in [1,2]. The center then responds to two actions at least 1 by choosing 2, and each leaf responds to that center by choosing 2. Thus the capped game has the unique equilibrium (2,2,2). A resource constraint has restored existence by changing the model. There is no claim that this cap maximizes welfare.

7. Unique best replies can have many intersections

Worked case 5: two substitutes, three parameter regions

Let two people choose xi≥0 with ui=xi−xi2/2−γxixj, j≠i, and γ≥0. The pure best reply is max{0,1−γxj}. We now solve every activity pattern. Both actions cannot be zero, because each would then choose 1. If only i is active, its action is 1 and the other best reply is zero exactly when γ≥1. If both are active,

x1+γx2=1,   γx1+x2=1.

Subtracting gives (1−γ)(x1−x2)=0. For γ≠1 the interior equilibrium is x1=x2=1/(1+γ), positive for every γ≥0. At γ=1 the two equations coincide. Combining the boundary and interior patterns gives the complete correspondence:

All pure equilibria of the two-agent substitute game
ParameterEquilibrium set
0≤γ<1Only (1/(1+γ),1/(1+γ))
γ=1All (z,1−z), 0≤z≤1
γ>1(1,0), (0,1), and (1/(1+γ),1/(1+γ))

At γ=1/2, the unique equilibrium is (2/3,2/3) with welfare 4/9. At γ=1, there is an entire segment, not just the two corners and the midpoint. At γ=2, the two specialized equilibria give welfare 1/2 each, while the interior equilibrium (1/3,1/3) gives only 1/9. The strict second derivative −1 guarantees a unique response to any fixed opponent action, yet says nothing by itself about how many times the two response curves intersect.

We can also solve the planner’s global problem without an interior-only first-order argument. Put S=x1+x2. Then

W=S−S2/2+(1−2γ)x1x2.

At γ=1/2 the product term vanishes, so every nonnegative pair with S=1 is a maximizer and the maximum is 1/2. At γ=1 or 2 the product coefficient is strictly negative. Therefore W≤S−S2/2≤1/2, with equality precisely when S=1 and x1x2=0: only (1,0) and (0,1). On the γ=1 equilibrium segment, W=[z2+(1−z)2]/2 ranges from 1/4 at z=1/2 to 1/2 at the endpoints. No probability over equilibria has been specified. Selecting the welfare-best equilibrium, predicting convergence to it, and estimating which one occurs are additional tasks.

8. Endogenous links, exact consent and collective gains

So far the network was fixed. Now let N={1,2,3}, and let g be any of the eight simple undirected graphs on N. Adding a link requires both endpoints’ consent; either endpoint may delete it. With 0<ρ<1 and c≥0, define

ui(g)=Σj≠i, connected to iρdg(i,j)−c·degreei(g).

The distance dg(i,j) is the number of edges on a shortest connecting path. Disconnected nodes generate no benefit. Each endpoint pays c for its own direct link, so aggregate resource cost is 2c per edge. A direct neighbor gives ρ, an indirect neighbor at distance two gives ρ2. This is the connections-model framework described by Jackson’s survey, revised 29 November 2003, with the original framework attributed there to Jackson and Wolinsky. We prove the complete three-node results rather than importing a general network classification.

A graph is pairwise stable if no endpoint strictly gains from deleting an existing edge, and no absent edge gives both endpoints weak gains with at least one strict gain. If both would be indifferent about adding an edge, its absence is allowed. Only one-edge deviations are tested. A graph is efficient here if it maximizes Σui across all eight graphs; this uses comparable utility units. Neither definition includes a formation path or a probability over networks.

All graph architectures and their total welfare
ArchitectureNumber of labeled graphsWelfare
Empty10
One edge32ρ−2c
Two-edge path34ρ+2ρ²−4c
Triangle16ρ−6c

Complete pairwise-stability proof. From empty, a new edge gives each endpoint ρ−c; hence empty is stable exactly when c≥ρ. In a one-edge graph, if c>ρ an endpoint wants to delete. If c≤ρ, connecting its endpoint to the isolated node gives the existing endpoint ρ−c≥0 and the isolated node ρ+ρ2−c>0; the absent edge therefore blocks. Thus no one-edge graph is stable.

In a path, the center gains c−ρ by deleting either edge; the affected leaf gains c−ρ−ρ2 by deleting its own edge. Adding the missing edge between the leaves gives each ρ−ρ2−c. All constraints hold exactly when ρ−ρ2≤c≤ρ. In a triangle, an endpoint deleting one edge retains an indirect connection to its former neighbor; the deletion gain is c−ρ+ρ2. Hence the triangle is stable exactly when c≤ρ−ρ2. This exhausts every graph. At c=ρ−ρ2, the triangle and all three paths are stable. At c=ρ, empty and all three paths are stable. Both equality conclusions depend on the stated weak/strict convention.

Complete efficiency proof. Triangle welfare minus path welfare is 2(ρ−ρ2−c). Path welfare is positive exactly when c<ρ+ρ2/2. A one-edge graph cannot be a maximizer: if c≤ρ, path welfare exceeds its welfare by 2(ρ+ρ2−c)>0; if c>ρ it has negative welfare and empty is better. Thus the efficient architecture is triangle below ρ−ρ2, path between that threshold and ρ+ρ2/2, and empty above the latter. At the first threshold triangle and all three paths tie; at the second empty and all three paths tie. “A unique architecture” is different from one unique labeled graph.

Worked case 6: pay the center, then ask how the network gets built

Take ρ=3/5. At c=1/2 the three paths are exactly the stable and efficient graphs. Their leaf–center–leaf payoffs are (23/50,1/5,23/50), totaling 28/25. Welfare by architecture, from empty through triangle, is (0,1/5,28/25,3/5).

Raise c to 7/10, keeping the benefit parameter fixed. Empty is now the only pairwise-stable graph, but the three paths are efficient. A path gives (13/50,−1/5,13/50), totaling 8/25. The center would delete a link, even though the network creates positive aggregate value. The architecture welfare vector is now (0,−1/5,8/25,−3/5). The three relevant cost thresholds are (6/25,3/5,39/50): triangle–path efficiency, empty/path stability boundary, and path–empty efficiency.

A declared transfer contract. Designate node 2 as center. Whenever edge 12 exists, node 1 pays node 2 t=3/20; whenever edge 23 exists, node 3 pays node 2 the same amount. If a designated link is severed or absent, its payment stops. The undesignated edge 13 carries no transfer. This specifies payments for every graph, including deviations, rather than only at the target. Each person starts with 2 cash units. Maintenance costs and payments are settled before network benefits: a leaf’s maximum cash obligation is 2c+t=31/20<2, and the center’s maintenance bill is at most 2c=7/5<2 even before receiving the transfers. The benefit terms are not used to prefund these bills. Link costs consume resources; only the side payments sum to zero.

At path {12,23}, net incremental payoffs become (11/100,1/10,11/100), still totaling 8/25. If the center deletes one edge, it retains one direct neighbor and one payment, so its payoff falls to 3/5−7/10+3/20=1/20. Its gain from retaining the edge is therefore 1/20. A leaf deleting its edge becomes isolated, stops paying and obtains zero, losing 11/100. Adding edge 13 changes neither transfer; each leaf’s payoff change is -23/50. The designated path is pairwise stable under the contract, and all three players prefer its simultaneous package to empty.

Yet empty is still pairwise stable. Its first link between two previously isolated nodes has aggregate gain 2ρ−2c=-1/5. Any balanced transfer between those two endpoints leaves this sum unchanged, so it cannot make both weakly better off. Under the particular contract a center–leaf first link gives 1/20 to the center but −1/4 to the leaf; edge 13 gives −1/10 each. None is a mutually attractive start. Reaching the desirable path therefore requires permission for a coordinated three-party package, or a separately specified intertemporal financing and formation protocol. A subsidy or side-payment calculation does not itself establish that such a protocol exists.

9. What evidence would justify using a design?

These models make logical claims conditional on rights, preferences, information and costs. A complete placement list may be infeasible in a real interface; an institutional priority may be legally constrained; a payment may be unenforceable; an apparent network neighbor may share an unobserved environment rather than cause someone’s behavior. None of those issues is resolved by solving a fixed point. Keep the design report explicit about feasible messages, what is verified, who can refuse, when money is available, what a link permits and how a deviation changes future obligations.

A raw association between neighbors’ actions does not identify β or γ. Actions are simultaneously chosen, network membership may respond to preferences or expected gains, and common shocks may move both endpoints. A causal study must supply an assignment or identification argument, respect spillovers in the treatment definition, measure links and costs at the relevant date, and deal with multiplicity or a stated selection rule. The same observed graph can be consistent with several payoff and formation models. Theoretical comparative statics are not empirical estimates.

Reproduction. The preference tables, value matrix, exact best-response equations and graph payoff law above supply the inputs. A reader can enumerate partial bijections and blocking pairs, sum the price certificate, solve the small rational systems, and calculate shortest-path benefits for the eight graphs. The companion editorial checks reconstruct these finite quantities independently; they are not represented here as an unavailable reader download. Finite checks complement the universal proofs and do not replace them.

10. Exercises

  1. DA foundations. In finite strict one-to-one matching with incomplete lists, prove termination, individual rationality, stability, the first rejected achievable-pair lemma and proposer optimality. Derive schedule independence. Identify why the last conclusion alone cannot prove truthful reporting.
  2. The incomplete market. For Worked case 1, find every stable matching and every applicant menu including outside. Explain the count of 21 individually rational partial matchings. Remove C; then, in a separate experiment with C present, reverse Z’s priority. Give both outcomes and distinguish these changes from a unilateral applicant report.
  3. The complete incentive argument. Prove the finite unmatched-set lemma with the no-cycle step. Then derive both menu inclusion and exclusion using a singleton report, a strictly-above truncation and coupled DA runs. Conclude strategy-proofness for every ordered-subset report, including an empty list and false acceptability. Do not assume the incentive theorem at any intermediate step.
  4. A recipient’s report and a list cap. Reconstruct the complete stable set in Worked case 2. Trace X’s specified false order. Under a one-name cap compare D’s sincere report [X] with [W]; under a two-name cap use sincere first-two lists. State precisely which of these changes the applicant incentive theorem covers.
  5. Certify the whole assignment set. Prove the nonnegative (u,p) upper bound for an arbitrary finite allowed-edge partial assignment. State the additional equalities needed for attainment with unsold objects and unmatched buyers. Apply it to Worked case 3, establish uniqueness, and reconcile all buyer and seller cash and utility increments.
  6. A forbidden pair. In Worked case 3 forbid B–Z. Find all maximizing assignments, verify the new price/utility certificate on every allowed edge, and explain why its failure on B–Z is irrelevant. Compare these supporting prices with zero prices. Do not invoke an unproved price-existence or integrality theorem.
  7. Existence without compactness. Derive the complete nonnegative best reply for the fixed-coefficient quadratic game. Prove the row-sum contraction result by a geometric Cauchy argument, including uniqueness. Calculate the β=1/4 path equilibrium and every person’s payoff. Explain why strict own-action concavity alone is insufficient for unique Nash equilibrium.
  8. Efficient action and who pays. Prove the β=1/4 planner optimum globally using the displayed quadratic form. For the [0,4] implementation variant, prove every-profile funding feasibility, budget balance and unique equilibrium of the fee/subsidy rule. Reconstruct charges, subsidies, final cash and net utility at the target. Is adoption a voluntary Pareto improvement relative to the original Nash outcome?
  9. Two changes in feedback and one cap. Solve the unbounded complementary path for all β≥0 and identify its exact finite-equilibrium boundary. Specialize to β=3/5 and β=3/4. Explain the difference between failure of the sufficient row bound and actual nonexistence. At β=3/4 impose cap 2 and prove the complete equilibrium set.
  10. All substitute equilibria. Solve every activity pattern of the two-agent game for all γ≥0. For γ=1/2,1,2 give the complete pure equilibrium and global planner sets, their welfare values or ranges, and a reason an interior linear solve alone would be incomplete.
  11. All graphs, all boundaries. For arbitrary 0<ρ<1 and c≥0 classify all eight three-node graphs under the chapter’s pairwise-stability and efficiency definitions. Prove the complete classification and equality cases. Specialize the welfare and stable sets to ρ=3/5,c=1/2 and 7/10. Distinguish architecture from labeled uniqueness.
  12. A financed design and a referee report. Verify every cash and edge-deviation claim for the 3/20 transfer contract in Worked case 6. Prove why balanced bilateral first-link transfers cannot start an improving path from empty at c=7/10. Then assess the claim: “We observe a stable network, so it is efficient and the positive correlation in neighbor actions proves a positive causal spillover.” Supply a corrected model statement and a feasible evidence plan. Use the rubric in the solution; disagreement about a policy choice is not a grading error.
Complete solutions and research-critique rubric

  1. A proposer never repeats an ordered pair, giving at most |A||H| proposals. It proposes only above outside and recipients hold only acceptable offers, proving individual rationality. Recipient holds only improve. A blocking applicant must have proposed to its preferred blocking institution and been rejected; that institution’s final partner is then strictly better, a contradiction.

    For proposer optimality, suppose the first rejected achievable pair is (a,h), and choose a stable ν containing it. Institution h keeps b whom it prefers to a. If b preferred ν(b) to h, b had already proposed to and been rejected by ν(b), an earlier achievable rejection. Equality is impossible because ν assigns h to a. If ν(b) is outside, the proposed h is strictly better. Hence b prefers h to ν(b), making (b,h) block ν. No achievable rejection is possible. Every applicant consequently receives at least its partner in every stable matching. Two legal DA schedules both produce such a stable optimum; strict preferences make each applicant’s partner identical, so the outcomes agree. A lie changes the reported profile and its stable set; comparison only within the old stable set cannot exclude the lie’s outcome. The menu argument, not this last comparison alone, closes that gap.

  2. The A,B–X,Y submarket has one empty, four one-pair and two full partial matchings, totaling seven. Z may be empty, with C or with D, giving 7·3=21 individually rational partial matchings. Stability forces C–Z: if Z holds D or nobody, C–Z blocks. It also forces a complete A,B assignment to X,Y. Both possible bijections are stable: μ=(A–X,B–Y,C–Z,D–∅) and ν=(A–Y,B–X,C–Z,D–∅). APDA produces μ and IPDA produces ν.

    Remove A for its menu computation: in IPDA, B prefers Y to X, so it holds Y and rejects X. Thus X is empty, Y–B and Z–C; X would accept A rather than outside, and Y ranks A above B. A’s menu is {∅,X,Y}. Remove B: A holds X and rejects Y, so X–A, Y empty and Z–C; X ranks B above A, and Y ranks B above outside, giving B the same menu. Remove C: Z gets D and would prefer C, giving C {∅,Z}. Remove D: Z gets C and would reject D, giving D only {∅}. Other institutions find C and D unacceptable. Outside is included even for an applicant normally matched.

    For the changed APDA experiments, removing C yields (A–X,B–Y,D–Z). Keeping C but reversing Z’s priority yields (A–X,B–Y,C–∅,D–Z). The first changes the participant set and the second changes the institution’s order. The strategy-proofness theorem instead fixes both when comparing D’s reports.

  3. Suppose stable μ leaves m0 unmatched while stable ν gives it h0. Stability of μ forces h0 to hold a preferred m1; stability of ν forces m1 to obtain a preferred h1; repeat with hk=ν(mk) and mk+1=μ(hk). Each partner exists because outside is worse than the preceding acceptable partner. A first repeat mk+1=mj cannot have j=0 because m0 is μ-unmatched. If j>0, injectivity forces hk=hj−1 and then mk=mj−1, an earlier repeat. A finite set cannot support this endless distinct path. Swap the matchings and then the sides to obtain identical unmatched sets.

    Hold others fixed and define Si as outside plus all IPDA offers when i rejects everything. Deleting futile offers to i produces IPDA without i, so Si={∅}∪{h:i≻hν−i(h)}. This is independent of i’s report. For any APDA partner h*≠∅, the full APDA outcome remains stable after replacing i’s list by [h*]. The unmatched-set lemma makes i matched in singleton IPDA, necessarily to h*. Singleton and reject-all runs coincide until h*’s first offer, so h* is in Si.

    Next delete h* and all lower names from i’s APDA report. Reproduce the full APDA execution up to just before i proposes to h*. All previous proposals and rejections are unchanged; i then has exhausted the truncated list and remains unmatched while others finish. If h*=∅, the original completed run already supplies the unmatched outcome. The lemma makes i unmatched in truncated IPDA. A receiver never loses acceptable matched status once acquired; hence no offer on the truncated list occurs. Couple truncated and reject-all IPDA up to a putative first such offer: their responses would coincide, so neither receives one. Thus the fixed menu has no reported-better outcome than h*.

    Every report therefore selects its best element of the same Si. Truth selects its true best element and no misreport improves it. Outside is always a feasible menu member, selected by the empty report. A falsely acceptable name may be in Si, but truth places it below outside; it cannot be a gain relative to the truthful maximum. These arguments assume neither incentive compatibility nor a general capacity-market unmatched theorem.

  4. All stable matchings must be full because lists are complete and the two sides have equal size. D cannot receive X, because A prefers X to every other institution and X prefers A to D. D cannot receive Y or Z, because D and W would block. Thus D–W is forced. For the six assignments of X,Y,Z to A,B,C, XYZ and YZX pass every pair test; XZY, YXZ, ZXY and ZYX are blocked by (C,X), (B,Z), (A,X) and (A,Y), respectively. These exhaust the stable set.

    Under X’s lie C,D,A,B, start with A–X,B–Y,C–Z and D approaching X. X prefers D to A under its report, releasing A. The sequence A→Y, B→Z, C→X, D→W gives (A–Y,B–Z,C–X,D–W). In X’s true order C is above A, so X has gained. Recipients are not the strategy-proof side of APDA.

    With one-name sincere lists, D is rejected at X and has no further permitted name. Reporting [W] instead yields W, which D prefers to outside. At a two-name cap D may list X,W; A,B,C list X,Y; Y,Z; Z,X, respectively, and APDA again yields (A–X,B–Y,C–Z,D–W). The theorem compares every possible ordered-subset report with the full true ordered list, holding the institution profile fixed. It does not promise that an unavailable full type can be reported under a one-name cap, nor cover a change by X in the opposite side’s strategy domain.

  5. For any partial matching M, sum ui+pj≥vij over its chosen edges. Each matched buyer and sold object appears once. Nonnegativity lets us add the unused u and p terms, yielding ΣMv≤Σu+Σp. Equality requires assigned edges to bind and unmatched buyers’ u and unsold objects’ p to vanish. These conditions suffice to certify the global maximum; every buyer’s chosen surplus attains its nonnegative bound, and nonnegative prices support sellers with zero retention values.

    In case 3, p=(5,2,0),u=(7,5,7). The slack rows ui+pj−vij are (0,1,5), (0,1,0), (8,0,0). Assignment A–X/B–Z/C–Y uses only zero slacks and attains 26. The six full values are 25,26,25,17,21,12; positivity permits any incomplete matching to be extended with extra positive value, so only that one full assignment maximizes. All 34 partial matchings are covered, without a claim about an arbitrary fractional relaxation.

    Buyer payments are (5,0,2), seller receipts in object order are (5,2,0), and buyer final cash is (15,20,18). Their sum with receipts is 60, the initial cash. Buyer utility increments are (7,5,7), total 19; seller receipts total 7; transfers cancel from total surplus, giving 26. Object Z’s zero price is compatible with its owner’s stipulated indifference about retention.

  6. The two maximizing assignments are A–X/B–Y/C–Z and A–Y/B–X/C–Z, both worth 25. With p=(6,2,0),u=(6,4,7), slack rows are (0,0,4), (0,0,−1), (9,0,0). The only negative slack is on B–Z, precisely the forbidden edge. Every allowed edge satisfies the bound; both proposed assignments attain Σu+Σp=17+8=25. Completeness follows from the certificate and its equality graph: C must take Z in a full binding assignment, and A,B must split X,Y in either order. A partial binding assignment cannot attain the total bound because every u is positive and at least one unmatched buyer would leave positive slack in the summation bound. Hence these two are all maxima among the 27 allowed partial matchings.

    At zero prices, A and B both uniquely demand X and C demands Y. Giving someone a less-valued object to complete a feasible allocation does not make it a demanded allocation. The supporting prices change those private comparisons, with actual payments going to the owners. This is a direct verification of one certificate, not a deduction from a general price-existence or integrality theorem.

  7. With others fixed, write k=ai+Σbijxj. The objective is kxi−xi2/2=k2/2−(xi−k)2/2, so the unique nonnegative maximizer is max(0,k). The max operator is 1-Lipschitz, and the row triangle inequality gives ||R(x)−R(y)||∞≤q||x−y||∞. If q<1, successive iteration increments are bounded by qkd. Summing the geometric tail makes the sequence Cauchy; each coordinate has a real nonnegative limit. Continuity makes that limit fixed. Two fixed points have distance at most q times itself and hence zero. No compact-domain existence theorem was used.

    At β=1/4, leaves satisfy l=1+m/4 and the center m=1+l/2. Therefore l=10/7 and m=12/7. At the positive best replies ui=xi2/2, giving (50/49,72/49,50/49), sum 172/49. Strict own concavity makes R a function; it does not make that function a contraction. The γ=1 substitute game, with a continuum of fixed points despite own curvature −1, is an explicit counterexample to the stronger claim.

  8. W=1′x−x′Qx/2, Q=I−G/2. The sum-of-squares identity in the text makes Q positive definite. Solving Qx*=1 yields (3,4,3). Expanding W around x* cancels the linear term, leaving W(x*)−W(x)=(x−x*)′Q(x−x*)/2≥0, with equality only at x*. Thus the optimum is global on the orthant and remains so under cap 4. W(x*)=10−17+12=5.

    In the policy variant x∈[0,4]3, s=(1,3/2,1), and each charge is half the other two subsidies. Its maxima are (5,4,5), below each payer’s initial 10; collect first, distribute second. Summing charges counts every subsidy twice at half weight, proving budget balance at every profile. The charge does not depend on its own payer’s xi, so the marginal incentive adds si. The capped best-response map is still 1/2-Lipschitz. At (3,4,3) its untruncated targets are exactly (3,4,3); hence that is its unique equilibrium.

    Gross utility increments are (3/2,2,3/2); subsidies (3,6,3); charges (9/2,3,9/2). Net transfers are (−3/2,3,−3/2), final cash (17/2,13,17/2), and net increments (0,5,0). The pool ends at zero and aggregate cash is 30. Endpoints previously obtained 50/49 each, so they lose. The planner gain 5−172/49=73/49 is an aggregate improvement, not a voluntary Pareto improvement. Compulsory enforceability and the stated funding/action bounds are substantive assumptions.

  9. Because β≥0, every best reply in the unbounded game is at least 1; all equilibrium coordinates are positive. The leaves coincide at l=1+βm, and m=1+2βl. Thus (1−2β2)l=1+β. If β<1/√2, l=(1+β)/(1−2β2) and m=(1+2β)/(1−2β2) are positive and uniquely solve the full best replies. If β≥1/√2, a positive l cannot solve the equation: its left side is nonpositive and right side positive. There is no finite equilibrium, including at equality.

    At β=3/5 this gives (40/7,55/7,40/7). The row bound is 6/5, so our sufficient contraction theorem is silent, but direct algebra proves unique equilibrium. At β=3/4 the algebraic vector is (−14,−20,−14), excluded by both nonnegativity and the strictly positive best replies. Now change the action set to [0,2]. Every clipped best reply is in [1,2]. At any equilibrium the center must be min{2,1+(3/4)(x1+x3)}=2 because both leaves are at least 1. Each leaf then chooses min{2,1+(3/4)2}=2. The vector (2,2,2) indeed satisfies the replies, establishing existence and uniqueness under the changed cap.

  10. With no active player, each wants to choose 1, so (0,0) is not an equilibrium. With only one active player, that player chooses 1 and the inactive one’s best reply is zero exactly when γ≥1. With both active, subtract the two linear equations to obtain (1−γ)(x1−x2)=0. For γ≠1 the unique interior solution is (1/(1+γ),1/(1+γ)); for γ=1 every positive pair summing to one solves them. Add the admissible boundary patterns to obtain exactly the three parameter regions in the table.

    At γ=1/2 the unique Nash profile is (2/3,2/3), each utility 2/9 and total 4/9. Planner welfare is S−S2/2, whose complete maximum set is every nonnegative pair with S=1 and value 1/2. At γ=1 the Nash set is (z,1−z), 0≤z≤1; its welfare [z2+(1−z)2]/2 ranges from 1/4 to 1/2. Since the planner’s extra term −x1x2 is strictly negative when both are positive, its maxima are only (1,0),(0,1), value 1/2. At γ=2, the Nash set is those same corners and (1/3,1/3), with welfare 1/2,1/2 and 1/9. The planner’s extra term is −3x1x2, so its maxima remain the two corners. An invertible interior solve misses the corner equilibria for γ>1, and at γ=1 the singular system must be analyzed for its complete continuum. No mixed-strategy or adjustment-process claim was requested or established.

  11. The four architectures exhaust the eight labeled graphs with multiplicities 1,3,3,1. From empty each endpoint’s addition gain is ρ−c, so stability requires c≥ρ. A lone edge is deleted if c>ρ. Otherwise a missing link to the isolated player gives gains ρ−c≥0 and ρ+ρ2−c>0, so it is never stable. In a path, center and leaf deletion gains are c−ρ and c−ρ−ρ2, while each missing-edge gain is ρ−ρ2−c. Thus precisely ρ−ρ2≤c≤ρ supports paths. In a triangle each deletion gain is c−ρ+ρ2, so stability requires c≤ρ−ρ2. These tests include every allowed one-link deviation.

    For efficiency, the welfare values are 0, 2ρ−2c, 4ρ+2ρ2−4c and 6ρ−6c. If a single edge has nonnegative value, c≤ρ and a path exceeds it by at least 2ρ2>0; otherwise empty beats it. Triangle exceeds path exactly below c=ρ−ρ2. A path exceeds empty exactly below c=ρ+ρ2/2. Thus below the first threshold only triangle is efficient; at it triangle and all three paths tie; between thresholds all three paths maximize; at the second threshold empty and all three paths tie; above it only empty maximizes. At the distinct stability threshold c=ρ, empty and all three paths are stable because both-indifferent additions need not occur.

    For ρ=3/5, the thresholds are 6/25,3/5,39/50. At c=1/2 the welfare vector is (0,1/5,28/25,3/5), and exactly the three paths are both stable and efficient. At c=7/10 the vector is (0,−1/5,8/25,−3/5): only empty is stable, whereas all three paths are efficient. A unique path architecture leaves three possible choices of the labeled center; it is not one unique labeled outcome.

  12. At path {12,23}, each leaf has gross benefit ρ+ρ2=24/25, pays c=7/10 and transfers 3/20, giving 11/100. The center has benefit 2ρ=6/5, pays 2c=7/5 and receives 3/10, giving 1/10. Transfer receipts exactly equal transfer payments. Each starts with 2: a leaf can pay at most 2c+t=31/20 at any graph, and the center can prefund its maximum 7/5 maintenance bill without relying on receipts. At the target, final cash before benefits is (23/20,9/10,23/20), totaling 16/5 after the 14/5 resource cost. Benefits are not assumed available to finance these payments.

    Deleting a center–leaf edge leaves the center with ρ−c+t=1/20, so it loses 1/20; the detached leaf falls to zero and loses 11/100. Adding the leaf–leaf edge gives each ρ−ρ2−c=−23/50 and changes neither designated payment. The path is pairwise stable. Empty remains stable: a first designated link gives (center,leaf)=(1/20,−1/4), and an undesignated first link gives (−1/10,−1/10). More generally every balanced transfer across a first link preserves the combined −1/5 surplus, ruling out weak gains for both. A three-party simultaneous package can give all three positive gains, but that is a different permitted move.

    Illustrative referee assessment. “The observations do not establish either conclusion. In the stated three-node model the high-cost empty graph is pairwise stable and inefficient. Stability restricts particular consent-based deviations, while efficiency compares all feasible graphs and requires comparable payoffs. A positive neighbor association is also consistent with selection into links, a common environment, or simultaneous responses. Specify whose behavior changes when a link or policy changes, the reporting and formation rules, enforceability and the dates of actual payments. Then use plausibly exogenous assignment or a defended structural identification argument, measure costs and links before the outcome, address spillovers and anticipation, and explain how multiple equilibria enter the prediction. Report sensitivity to the action cap, outside option and transfer protocol rather than presenting a computed equilibrium as uniquely observed.”

    20-point rubric. Award 4 for the state-contingent transfer and complete funded cash account; 4 for all deletion/addition margins with the exact consent convention; 3 for the first-link impossibility and changed coordination right; 4 for distinguishing stability, welfare, selection and causal interpretation using a valid counterexample; and 5 for a feasible evidence plan that addresses at least assignment/selection, common shocks or simultaneous actions, measurement/timing and spillovers. Credit a different defensible design if its rights and funding are complete. An invented payer, double-counted transfer or assertion that correlation proves causation must be corrected before the corresponding domain is passed.

11. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. In three minutes explain why the word “best” means something different for an applicant, an assignment planner and a network policymaker. Include an outside option, one payment recipient and one excluded deviation.

Model explanation

For an applicant, truthful APDA selects its true best outcome from a menu determined by everyone else’s reports and the institution priorities; outside is in the menu, so truth does not force an unacceptable assignment. Proposer optimality within a fixed stable set is only one part of the proof. For the monetary assignment planner, “best” means the highest total value over feasible one-unit assignments; nonnegative prices and buyer utility bounds certify it, and the object’s owner actually receives the buyer’s payment. For a network policymaker, aggregate welfare includes effects on neighbors. A funded policy can improve that sum while hurting some participants, and a profitable three-party package can be unavailable when only bilateral link additions are permitted. The comparison changes if the allowed reports, cash, actions or deviations change.

Delayed retention. Revisit without the worked calculations: (a) Why must the menu run propose from the institution side? (b) What term changes between the network potential and aggregate welfare? (c) Can failure of a row-sum contraction bound establish nonexistence? (d) At the high-cost empty network, why can a balanced transfer not make the first link mutually attractive?

Answers

(a) The proved construction uses institution-proposing DA with i rejecting all offers. Singleton and truncated reports are coupled in that direction because i is a receiver who can never return to unmatched after accepting an acceptable offer. Replacing that run by applicant-proposing DA would require a different argument and can produce the wrong menu. (b) For the symmetric quadratic game, the potential is 1′x−x′(I−βG)x/2; welfare is 1′x−x′(I−2βG)x/2 because each link affects both endpoints. (c) No: β=3/5 gives the unique positive (40/7,55/7,40/7) although the row bound is 6/5. Direct equations establish the actual failure threshold 1/√2 in the unbounded path. (d) Its combined first-link gain is −1/5. A balanced transfer changes its division, not its sum, so both endpoints cannot weakly gain. The three-party package exploits an indirect benefit absent from the first isolated link.

12. Scope, sources and the next step

The finite matching theorem includes all strict ordered-subset reports and outside options. The assignment argument verifies supplied certificates rather than proving a general price-existence theorem. Network results concern the specified pure-action games and three-node formation model; no equilibrium-selection distribution, general capacity/tie matching result, causal coefficient or dynamic formation theorem is imported. All preference profiles, valuation numbers, policy budgets and exercises are original.

The inspected primary scopes are Manea’s strict-matching definitions and rejection argument; the noncircular menu proof in Appendix B of the dated Gonczarowski–Heffetz–Thomas preprint; Pass’s unit-demand and price-welfare model; the linear best replies and active-set conditions in Bramoullé–Kranton–D’Amours; and the connections-model and pairwise-consent definitions in Jackson’s revised survey. An inspected survey by an originator is not a claim to have inspected every original article it cites. The results used here have been proved at the scope stated in the text.

Continue to Theory synthesis and research critique, where model choice, theorem hypotheses, proof completeness and economically meaningful counterexamples become the object of a structured referee report.

Sources and further study

  • Mihai Manea — MIT 14.16 Matching Theory (based on slides by Fuhito Kojima), 2016 — Strict one-to-one matching, DA existence/proposer optimality and scope of proposer truthfulness.
  • Yannai A. Gonczarowski, Ori Heffetz and Clayton Thomas — Strategyproofness-Exposing Descriptions of Matching Mechanisms — Noncircular fixed-menu route to individual proposer strategy-proofness. Chapter supplies the finite unmatched-set lemma, schedule coupling and truncation-prefix details rather than invoking them without proof.
  • Rafael Pass — A Course in Networks and Markets, Chapter 8: Matching Markets — Assignment utility and ownership accounting; our direct nonnegative price/utility upper bound gives a complete certificate for all feasible partial assignments, including a forbidden edge.
  • Yann Bramoullé, Rachel Kranton and Martin D’Amours — Strategic Interaction and Networks — Economic interpretation of complements/substitutes and boundary active-set logic. Our finite path/two-agent solutions, contraction proof, planner square completion and funding incidence are derived independently.
  • Matthew O. Jackson — A Survey of Models of Network Formation: Stability and Efficiency — Primary exposition by a co-originator of the connections model, attributed there to Jackson–Wolinsky (1996). Our three-node all-graph classification, equality boundaries and contract-conditioned transfers are proved directly.
